**Yes—browser-use is worth testing, but I would fix deadline handling and evidence handoffs before committing to a migration.** It could reduce browser-navigation overhead; it will not automatically solve the validation failures that prevented submission.

I inspected the current code and browser-use documentation. I couldn’t retrieve the linked run or find its log locally, so the run-specific assessment relies on your summary.

Browser-use offers several relevant features:

| Capability | Potential benefit here |
|---|---|
| Multiple actions per model step | Fewer model round trips for routine interactions |
| Configurable vision and fast mode | Potentially less screenshot and reasoning overhead |
| Structured output | More consistent specialist reports |
| Existing-browser CDP connection | Can potentially use the challenge’s supplied browsers |

These are documented in its [agent settings](https://docs.browser-use.com/open-source/customize/agent/all-parameters) and [browser settings](https://docs.browser-use.com/open-source/customize/browser/all-parameters). **Whether they improve this workflow needs measurement with your required model and proxy.**

The current code exposes more immediate opportunities:

1. **Establish why this run had such a short effective budget.**  
   The default is 1,185 seconds, but [`run_seconds()`](/home/omran/Projects/EHL_Finale/src/hackathon_toolkit/rfq/runtime.py:916) shortens it to the platform’s `expires_at`. The reported timing does not demonstrate that this attempt received a full 20 minutes. Log configured duration, platform expiry, startup time, and effective remaining budget together.

2. **Make model calls respect the remaining phase budget.**  
   [`ModelClient`](/home/omran/Projects/EHL_Finale/src/hackathon_toolkit/rfq/runtime.py:683) uses a 60-second HTTP timeout and up to three attempts, without receiving the remaining run budget. With about 65 seconds left, a slow call can consume practically all remaining time. Browser-use also has model and step timeouts, so adopting it still requires deliberate deadline configuration.

3. **Validate specialist handoffs before accepting their reports.**  
   Workers currently finish through a free-text `report`. Require structured findings, valid evidence IDs, and explicit missing prerequisites. The missing-evidence and exact-quote errors are evidence-contract failures; changing the browser driver alone won’t repair them. Preserve exact source excerpts in code so the model needn’t reconstruct them.

4. **Measure selective Clef checks.**  
   Your figures imply approximately **2.1 seconds per check**. Those costs overlap across workers, but awaited checks still delay each worker. Compare the current policy against checks focused on obstructions, failed actions, and uncertain states. Zero service failures establishes availability, not a speed benefit.

5. **Prove the submission sequence independently.**  
   The repository already has `--eligibility-first`. Establish repeatable review → TAN → signing → accepted submission before adding full research complexity. Then measure full-bid quality separately; a partial submission only validates the completion path.

**My recommendation:** first address those issues, then benchmark browser-use as a replacement for **one specialist’s navigation loop**. Keep the existing calculation, evidence, review, and receipt checks. Use the same model, equivalent tasks, and repeated runs; compare valid evidence collected, model calls, elapsed time, and eventual accepted submissions.

A full rewrite now would introduce substantial integration work without evidence that navigation is the dominant bottleneck. A bounded comparison would tell us whether browser-use earns that investment.
